components.description: Conditioning on a sub-sigma-algebra
components.source_items: Durrett pp. 205-208: the setting (Omega, F_o, P), a sub-sigma-field F and integrable X; conditions (i) F-measurability and (ii) equal integrals over every event of F; versions; equalities read almost surely (p. 206); P(A|G) = E(1_A|G) and E(X|Y) = E(X|sigma(Y)) (p. 208); the interpretive claim opening Section 4.1.1 (p. 207). Present: setting, both conditions, versions, almost-sure convention, P(B|G), E(X|Y), notation (lines 18-43); the reading of the conditioning sigma-algebra as specified information (lines 5-8).
components.gap: Supply the source's interpretive (justificatory) claim for this entry, Durrett p. 207 at the opening of Section 4.1.1: the conditioning sigma-algebra is read as the information at one's disposal, in that for each of its events one knows whether or not it occurred, and E(X|G) is read as the 'best guess' of the value of X given that information. The route states the definition and its almost-everywhere convention (conditional-expectation.tex lines 18-43) and calls the conditional expectation a variable measurable from specified information that preserves event integrals (lines 5-8), but nowhere states the best-guess reading of the definition; the mean-square minimization of thm:p15-conditional-l2-projection (lines 264-278) holds only for square-integrable X and is not presented as that reading.

components.description: Existence, integrability and almost-everywhere uniqueness

components.source_items: Lemma 4.1.1 with its proof through A = {Y > 0} (p. 206); uniqueness through A = {Y - Y' >= eps} (p. 206); the Radon-Nikodym theorem as used (pp. 206-207); existence for X >= 0 with mu = P, nu(A) = integral of X over A, then X = X+ - X- (p. 207). All present with written steps: integrability bound and uniqueness (annex lines 5-21), density construction on (Omega, G) without completion (annex lines 23-41), proved Radon-Nikodym theorem (radon-nikodym.tex lines 208-221).

components.description: Linearity, order, known information and locality
components.source_items: Theorem 4.1.9(a)(b) with proofs (pp. 210-211); Example 4.1.3 with the constant case (p. 207); Example 4.1.4 with its independence definition and proof (p. 208); Theorem 4.1.2 with proof (p. 206); identity (4.1.5) (p. 212). All these statements and proofs are present. Omitted: the methodological claim of Example 4.1.4, the interpretive glosses of Examples 4.1.3 and 4.1.4, and the framing claim opening Section 4.1.2.
components.gap: Supply the source's claims attached to this entry that the route omits: (a) the methodological claim of Example 4.1.4 (Durrett p. 208) that here and in the sequel conditional expectations are found by 'guess and verify', proposing a formula and then checking it against conditions (i) and (ii) of the definition; (b) the interpretive glosses of Examples 4.1.3 and 4.1.4 (pp. 207-208): when X is known (measurable from the information) the best guess for X is X itself, and when nothing about X is known (X independent of the information) the best guess is its mean EX; (c) the framing claim opening Section 4.1.2 (p. 210) that conditional expectation has many of the properties of ordinary expectation. thm:p15-conditional-basic (conditional-expectation.tex lines 59-79) and its annex (annex lines 45-83) state and prove every linearity, expectation, order, absolute-value, known-information, independence, locality and probability-bound assertion, but contain none of (a)-(c).

components.description: Nonnegative extension and conditional convergence theorems
components.source_items: Theorem 4.1.9(c), Xn >= 0 increasing to X with EX finite, with proof (pp. 210-211); the remark deriving the decreasing case from it under E|Y1|, E|Y| finite (p. 210). Present: the increasing case for the nonnegative extension, which agrees with the integrable definition when EX is finite (lines 84-96); the decreasing variant with the source's route through Y1 - Yn and a model showing E|Y1| finite cannot be dropped (w02b-p15-008 lines 303-335, annex lines 325-435); the worked boundary on null modifications.

components.description: Conditional Jensen and the source's countable affine approximation
components.source_items: Theorem 4.1.10 with E|X|, E|phi(X)| finite; the linear case set aside; the countable rational set S with phi as supremum of its lines; the remark that one exceptional set per pair forces a countable supremum (p. 211). All present, with the approximation fact proved in the annex rather than cited.

components.description: The L^p classes used here
components.source_items: L^p for p >= 1 in Theorem 4.1.11 (p. 211); L^2(F_o) as the square-integrable F_o-measurable variables in the remark after Theorem 4.1.15 (p. 213). Present, including L^infinity and the inner product on L^2.

components.description: Norms and contraction in every stated L^p
components.source_items: Theorem 4.1.11 with its proof from conditional Jensen and E(E(Y|F)) = EY, the latter read off condition (ii) with A = Omega (pp. 211-212). Present for 1 <= p <= infinity, with the norm properties proved.

components.description: Both tower identities and the measurable-version reduction
components.source_items: Theorem 4.1.12 with proof; Theorem 4.1.13 (i)(ii) with proof; the commentary on Theorem 4.1.13; the framing sentence introducing Theorems 4.1.12-4.1.14 (all p. 212). Statements and proofs present; the summary that the smaller sigma-field wins is entailed by the displayed identities. Omitted: the evaluative and cautionary commentary and the framing claim.
components.gap: Supply the source's commentary on Theorem 4.1.13 (Durrett p. 212) that the route omits: (a) the evaluative claim that the second identity, used together with Theorem 4.1.14 (taking out what is known), is a powerful tool for computing conditional expectations; (b) the cautionary claim that the source's author has seen that identity used several times to prove results that are false; (c) the framing claim introducing Theorems 4.1.12-4.1.14 that conditional expectation also has properties, like E(E(Y|F)) = EY, with no analogue for ordinary expectation. The remark at conditional-expectation.tex lines 180-181 that the nesting hypothesis is essential and that arbitrary conditioning sigma-algebras need not commute is a different claim and supplies none of (a)-(c).

components.description: Taking out a measurable multiplier
components.source_items: The lead-in that F-measurable variables behave like constants and can be taken outside (p. 212); Theorem 4.1.14 with E|Y|, E|XY| finite and its four-step proof (indicator, simple, nonnegative by monotone convergence, positive and negative parts) (pp. 212-213). Present, with the same four steps and the nonnegative extended form.

components.description: Finite and countable information partitions
components.source_items: Example 4.1.5: finite or countable partition into positive-probability cells, the cellwise average formula, its verification, the trivial sigma-field case, P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) and P(A|F) = P(A|Omega_i) on each cell, and the interpretive sentence on what the partition information tells (p. 208). Formula, null cells, trivial case, verification and recovery of the finite formula are present; P(A|A_i) on each positive cell appears in the annex Bayes proof (annex lines 613-616). Omitted: the interpretive sentence.
components.gap: Supply the source's interpretive claim for Example 4.1.5 (Durrett p. 208): the partition information tells which cell contains the outcome, and given that information the best guess for X is the average value of X over that cell. thm:p15-conditional-partitions (conditional-expectation.tex lines 199-211) and its annex (annex lines 343-372) give and prove the cellwise formula, its null-cell freedom and the trivial-sigma-algebra case, but state no such reading.

components.description: Writing a measurable quantity as a function of the observation
components.source_items: E(X|Y) = E(X|sigma(Y)) (p. 208); writing a sigma(Y)-measurable version as a function of Y, used in the proof of Theorem 4.1.18 (p. 215). Present with a full lift construction, the nonnegative and real cases, and almost-everywhere uniqueness under the law of Y.

components.description: Joint densities and integration over an independent coordinate
components.source_items: Example 4.1.6: joint density, positivity of the marginal integral assumed for simplicity, E|g(X)| finite, the formula for h, the heuristic that 'guesses' it, the verification, and the Remark dropping positivity (p. 209); Example 4.1.7: independent X, Y, E|phi(X,Y)| finite, g(x) = E phi(x,Y), proof by change of variables and product measure (pp. 209-210). Present: both formulas, with exceptional-section conventions, and both verifications. Omitted: the heuristic; the Remark's statement that every h with h(y) times the marginal integral equal to the integral of g(x)f(x,y) works.
components.gap: Supply (a) the source's justificatory heuristic for Example 4.1.6 (Durrett p. 209), introduced there as the link with the undergraduate definition: treating the density values as if they were probabilities gives the conditional density f(x,y) divided by the integral of f(x,y) dx, and integrating g against that conditional density gives E(g(X)|Y=y), which is how the formula is guessed before it is verified; and (b) the full variant stated in the source's Remark dropping the positivity assumption: any h satisfying h(y) times the integral of f(x,y) dx = the integral of g(x)f(x,y) dx gives the conditional expectation, so h may be anything where the marginal integral vanishes. thm:p15-conditional-density-formulas (conditional-expectation.tex lines 225-250) and its annex (annex lines 416-467) contain no heuristic derivation, and they state only the single choice h = 0 off D together with P(Y in D) = 1, not the source's freedom off D.

components.description: The complete L^2 space and its information subspace
components.source_items: Remark after Theorem 4.1.15: L^2(F_o) is a Hilbert space and L^2(F) is a closed subspace (p. 213). Present with completeness and closedness proved without completing the sigma-algebra.

components.description: Orthogonality and the exact prediction-error identity
components.source_items: Theorem 4.1.15 (EX^2 finite; E(X|F) minimizes the mean square error) with its proof through Theorem 4.1.14, Cauchy-Schwarz, the orthogonality identity and the Pythagorean expansion; the remark reading E(X|F) as the point of the closed subspace L^2(F) closest to X (p. 213). Present: orthogonality, the exact identity, unique minimizer among all G-measurable competitors; the closest-point reading is the minimizer statement (see defect_observations on the word projection).

components.description: Conditional variance
components.source_items: var(X|F) = E(X^2|F) - E(X|F)^2 (Exercise 4.1.7, p. 216). Present, with its identification as the conditional squared residual, nonnegativity, and a worked value 1/12.

components.description: Variance decomposition and the effect of additional information
components.source_items: Exercise 4.1.6: the nested identity for G inside F with EX^2 finite, and the reading of the inequality obtained by dropping the middle term, geometrically (larger subspace, closer projection) and statistically (more information, smaller mean square error); Exercise 4.1.7: the total-variance identity, presented as an important special case of Exercise 4.1.6 when G = {empty set, Omega} (p. 216). Present: both identities with proofs, the statistical reading (lines 308-309) and, by entailment, the geometric one. Omitted: the special-case relation.
components.gap: Supply the source's relational claim for Exercise 4.1.7 (Durrett p. 216): the total-variance identity Var(X) = E Var(X|F) + Var(E(X|F)) is an important special case of the nested prediction-error identity of Exercise 4.1.6, obtained when the smaller sigma-algebra is the trivial one {empty set, Omega}. thm:p15-conditional-variance (conditional-expectation.tex lines 290-310) states both identities, and its annex (annex lines 550-578) proves the total-variance identity directly, but neither states that it is this special case.

components.description: Conditional Chebyshev, Cauchy--Schwarz and Bayes identities
components.source_items: Exercise 4.1.1 (Bayes formula for G in the conditioning sigma-field and its reduction to the usual partition formula); Exercise 4.1.2 (conditional Chebyshev); Exercise 4.1.3 (conditional Cauchy-Schwarz by imitating the unconditional quadratic argument) (p. 216). All present; the proof of Cauchy-Schwarz follows the quadratic method; P(A) > 0 is stated.

components.description: Variance of an independent random sum
components.source_items: Exercise 4.1.8: Y_i iid with mean mu and variance sigma^2, N an independent positive-integer variable with EN^2 finite, X = Y_1 + ... + Y_N, var(X) = sigma^2 EN + mu^2 var(N), and the source's hint for understanding and remembering the formula (p. 216). The statement, the zero-count extension and the proof are present. Omitted: the hint and its two special cases.
components.gap: Supply the source's explanatory claim for Exercise 4.1.8 (Durrett p. 216): to understand and remember var(S) = sigma^2 EN + mu^2 var(N), consider the two special cases in which N is constant and in which Y is constant. thm:p15-conditional-random-sums (conditional-expectation.tex lines 329-341) and its annex (annex lines 620-658) state and prove the formula, including the zero-count case, but neither the hint nor those two special cases appears on the route.

components.description: When conditioning preserves the entire distribution
components.source_items: Exercise 4.1.9 (E(Y|G) = X with EY^2 = EX^2 finite implies X = Y) and Exercise 4.1.10 (same law under E|Y| finite implies equality, with the sign-agreement hint applied to Y - c) (pp. 216-217). Both present with written proofs following the shifted-sign route.

components.description: Noncommuting information, nonmultiplicativity and null observations
components.source_items: Exercise 4.1.5: an example on {a, b, c} with the two iterated conditional expectations unequal (p. 216); the entry's own nonmultiplicativity and null-observation models. All three models present with tables and defining identities.

components.description: Simultaneous conditional distributions
components.source_items: The entry is a proof boundary. It promises that the next chapter constructs one probability kernel for all target events and proves the integration formula, the source's sphere calculation with its alternative great-circle coordinates, and conditional Hoelder. Each promise is delivered with annex proofs: kernel construction (real, Borel-coded and observation-parametrized), Theorem 4.1.16 in both the everywhere and the source's almost-everywhere sense, the spherical model and its alternative coordinates, and Exercise 4.1.4 through the regular law of the pair. The rest of Section 4.1.3 belongs to ED26-P15-CH-regular-conditional-laws (see defect_observations).

defect_observations: Example 4.1.8 (Durrett p. 210, inside this unit's locator) is reached here only through the C021 boundary. The target chapter supplies the coordinate model and the density calculation (regular-conditional-laws.tex lines 195-248; annex lines 346-435). On the route, however, the example's name (Borel's paradox), the naive expectation that both angles should be uniform, and the explanation that the angle law is not uniform because there is more area near the equator than near the pole are all missing. A grep finds 'Borel paradox' only at bayes-factor-computation.tex line 1041. This affects ED26-P15-CH-regular-conditional-laws C010/C011. It is not counted against C021, whose boundary promises only the sphere calculation.

Durrett p. 214 says regular conditional distributions do not always exist, gives the history (Dieudonne 1948; Doob 1953, p. 624; Faden 1985) and explains that exceptional null sets pile up. On the route only the bare statement appears (conditioning-independence-and-information-w02b-p15-008.tex lines 235-239). The attribution and the explanation are in files not yet routed: conditioning-independence-and-information-w02c-p15-008.tex lines 12-19 and 237-244, and probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex lines 809-836. This belongs to ED26-P15-CH-regular-conditional-laws C002, which is recorded open, and does not change the C021 boundary verdict.

The routed existence proof (annex/p15/conditional-expectation.tex lines 23-40) moves from Radon-Nikodym densities against the restriction of P to G to integrals against P without writing that identification step. It also asserts absolute continuity without its one-line reason. The owner packet's file conditioning-independence-and-information-w02c-p15-007.tex (body lines 70-152, annex lines 15-217) writes both, but that file is not yet routed. The routed text matches the source's own level of detail (p. 207), so C002 is judged covered. This is recorded as a rigor observation only.

Three items are judged present by entailment, not by matching wording. (1) 'The smaller sigma-field wins' restates the two identities of thm:p15-conditional-tower. (2) The claim that F-measurable variables can be taken outside like constants is carried by the title and identity of thm:p15-conditional-pullout. (3) The geometric reading of Theorem 4.1.15 as projection onto L^2(F), with Figure 4.1, and the geometric reading of Exercise 4.1.6 are carried by thm:p15-conditional-l2-space (closed subspace) and thm:p15-conditional-l2-projection (orthogonality and closest point). The body never uses the word projection; the annex calls the result the 'H-projection identity' at line 569.

The locator pp. 205-217 also covers the Chapter 4 preamble on martingales (p. 205) and the opening of Section 4.2 (p. 217: the martingale definition, Example 4.2.1 and the superharmonic remark). No component of this unit selects that martingale material, so it was not assessed here.
